title: From Temple to study
hook: at Yavneh, Yochanan ben Zakkai rebuilds Jewish life around study and prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, Masada: a fortress on a desert rock, and a story still argued over. Your line was all looking at the same rock. Did you hear someone tell a story their way? Today, while Jerusalem is still under siege, a teacher gets out in a coffin. Day nine hundred one.

The coffin is carried to the city gate by two students, one at the head and one at the feet. The guards inside Jerusalem want to stab it, to be sure the body is dead. The students talk them out of it. Inside the coffin is their teacher, Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, very much alive. That's how the Talmud, in tractate Gittin, tells his escape from the besieged city. He has pretended to be sick, then pretended to die, because the zealots holding Jerusalem won't let anyone leave. Once outside, he walks to the Roman commander's tent with one request.
screen: `A COFFIN AT THE CITY GATE.` → `THE TEACHER INSIDE IS ALIVE.` → `HE WALKS TO THE ROMAN TENT.`

segments.voice: In the Talmud's story the Roman is Vespasian, soon to become emperor, and he tells the rabbi to ask him for something. Among his requests, Rabbi Yochanan asks, in paraphrase: give me Yavneh and its sages. Yavneh. Not Jerusalem. Not the Temple. A place to keep teaching. The Talmud doesn't pretend everyone agreed with him. It records a sharp objection: he should have asked Rome to spare Jerusalem itself. And it gives his reasoning: ask for that much, and he might not get even a little rescue. Now think about what had just been lost. Until then, Jewish worship had a center: one house, one altar, priests, offerings. With the Temple burned, what could take its place? At Yavneh, tradition says, the sages began to answer: study of Torah, and prayer. The Talmud links the daily prayers to the daily Temple offerings, so that the words a person says stand where the offering once stood. Long before, the prophet Hosea had already pointed this way: "Take with you words, and return unto the LORD." The same verse ends with an offering of a new kind; in the Hebrew, it is bulls of our lips. Words, in place of bulls. A sanctuary made of time and speech, which can be carried anywhere. In the rabbis' telling, that move, from Temple to study, is how a people without a Temple kept going. The house was gone. The conversation went on.
screen: `GIVE ME YAVNEH AND ITS SAGES.` · `SOME SAID HE SHOULD HAVE ASKED MORE.` · then, large: `TAKE WITH YOU WORDS.` · then: `A SANCTUARY YOU CAN CARRY.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to rebuild one thing after a loss. Sit, and breathe slowly. Choose something that changed and can't go back to the way it was: a job, a home, a routine, a friendship, a way your body used to work. Then ask Rabbi Yochanan's question. Not "how do I get the whole city back?" but "what is my Yavneh?" What is one small thing I can still build, here, that carries what mattered? Let one answer come. It can be very small. If you pray, you can take with you words, as Hosea says, and return. The bell holds the time.
Yavneh. The town Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai asked Rome for, where Jewish life was rebuilt around Torah study and prayer after the Temple fell. Today's word.
Your line: words, in place of bulls. Today, after something doesn't go your way, ask what your Yavneh is, and build that one small thing. Day nine hundred one.

screen: `DAY 901 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TABLE IS THE ALTAR.`

howItsDone: Jewish prayer services follow a daily rhythm that the Talmud connects to the Temple offerings, and Torah study, in a synagogue, a study hall or at home, is itself treated as a form of worship.

let me go home in peace.
fork.reveal: he asks for Yavneh and its sages. the Talmud records the objection that he should have asked for Jerusalem, and his answer: ask for too much and you may get nothing.

original.note: Hebrew: Yavneh, the town where, tradition says, the sages gathered after the Temple fell.

trapdoor: what you thought: the rabbis just kept going after the Temple fell.
what it means: Yochanan ben Zakkai asked for Yavneh and its sages, and Jewish life was rebuilt around study and prayer.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud records the criticism of his choice, and ties daily prayer to the daily offerings, words in place of bulls, as Hosea had said.

notes: Gittin 56a–b paraphrased: students (Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua) carry the coffin; guards want to pierce it; request 'give me Yavneh and its sages'; Rabbi Yosef's (or Rabbi Akiva's) objection; the answer that he might get nothing. Please check details.
'Prayer, three times a day' and the link to the daily offerings (Berakhot 26b) — confirm framing; Berakhot 26b also gives the patriarchs view.
Hosea quotation is KJV; 'the calves of our lips' paraphrased as 'so we will offer the calves of our lips'.
'Tradition says' is used for the program at Yavneh; Keeper may want to name specific takkanot.

Editor: Gittin 56b has three requests, so 'among his requests'; cut unsourced 'near the coast' and the 'three times a day at Yavneh' attribution; 'calves of our lips' is the same verse (Hosea 14:2), not later; cut the stock 'no army can burn a teaching' line; practice opener varied (day 899 also sat with a loss).

Auditor (2026-10-01): Hosea now quoted from JPS 1917 ('Take with you words, and return unto the LORD'), numbered as in the Hebrew; KJV's 'calves of our lips' replaced by the Hebrew sense 'bulls of our lips' (JPS 1917 renders it 'for bullocks the offering of our lips'). Gittin 56b gives the Talmud's reasoning, not a reply by Yochanan, so 'it even gives his answer' became 'it gives his reasoning'; cut the stock 'that honesty is part of the story' (the rabbis-keep-both-sides motif recurs on 897, 898, 903, 906).
